extracted.intended_audience: referees / peer reviewers for Communications Biology (Nature Portfolio)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for referees assessing manuscripts submitted to Communications Biology, covering criteria for publication, how to write and submit reviews, confidentiality, conflicts of interest, timing, anonymity, transparent peer review, and related editorial policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of results
rubrics_metrics.description: The results are novel (abstracts and internet preprints do not compromise novelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be published in Communications Biology a paper should meet several general criteria: novelty is required. If not novel, identify the major papers that compromise novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of evidence for conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper provides strong evidence for its conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should consider whether the claims are convincing; if not, specify what further evidence is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical soundness of data
rubrics_metrics.description: The data are technically sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors take technical criticisms very seriously; strong technical concerns should be clearly explained to the authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance to sub-field
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript is important to scientists in the specific sub-field of biology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In general, to be acceptable, a paper should represent an advance in understanding which may influence thinking in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance in understanding / conceptual advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper should represent an advance in understanding which may influence thinking in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers judged to be of insufficient interest to the field, or otherwise inappropriate, are rejected promptly without external review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the editors with the information needed to reach a decision and instruct authors on how they can strengthen their paper to the point where it may be acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A negative review should explain to the authors the weaknesses of their manuscript so rejected authors can understand the basis for the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional tone and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews are professional documents between peers and should not contain personal attacks, disparaging language, or otherwise inappropriate content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid saying anything that may cause needless offence; referees should be candid but professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential comments to the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential comments to the editor are welcome, but it is helpful if the main points are stated in the comments for transmission to the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential reviewer comments to the editor or any other correspondence between authors and reviewers and our office will not be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major claims identification
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the major claims of the paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal review should clearly state the paper's major claims to help the editor and authors understand the core contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty assessment / prior work identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims novel? If not, please identify the major papers that compromise novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should point out specific prior papers that reduce novelty and explain how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest to others in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the paper be of interest to others in the field?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the manuscript appeals beyond a very narrow audience in the sub-field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to influence thinking in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the paper influence thinking in the field?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the results change perspectives, methods, or open new avenues of research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincingness of claims / further evidence needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims convincing? If not, what further evidence is needed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify what additional experiments, analyses, controls, or data would be required to make the claims persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested additional experiments / their likely impact and difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there other experiments that would strengthen the paper further? How much would they improve it, and how difficult are they likely to be?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help editors judge whether suggested experiments are reasonable to request and whether they would materially change the validity or scope of conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualization within previous literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims appropriately discussed in the context of previous literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether authors have fairly cited and interpreted prior work and whether they have oversold their claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission potential / encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the manuscript is unacceptable in its present form, does the study seem sufficiently promising that the authors should be encouraged to consider a resubmission in the future?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate whether the problems are fixable and whether encouraging resubmission is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of writing and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the manuscript clearly written? If not, how could it be made more accessible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should suggest edits, reorganizations, or simplifications to improve communication of key findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / possibility to shorten
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the manuscript be shortened to aid communication of the most important findings?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise on sections that could be condensed or moved to supplementary material to sharpen the main narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overselling
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors done themselves justice without overselling their claims?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out instances where language or interpretation exaggerates the findings beyond the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair treatment of previous literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Have they been fair in their treatment of previous literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note missing citations or misrepresentations of earlier work and recommend corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological detail and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Have they provided sufficient methodological detail that the experiments could be reproduced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, request source code, detailed protocols, mathematical derivations, or other materials to enable replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of statistical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statistical analysis of the data sound?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify inappropriate statistical tests, lack of multiple-testing correction, inadequate sample-size justification, or other weaknesses in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting additional data or materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Should the authors be asked to provide further data or methodological information to help others replicate their work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: source code for modelling studies, detailed protocols or mathematical derivations; editors may obtain paywalled references if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any special ethical concerns arising from the use of animals or human subjects?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag ethical or regulatory issues clearly so editors can investigate or request documentation (e.g., ethics approvals, consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer selection is based on many factors, including expertise, reputation, specific recommendations and previous experience of a reviewer's characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may avoid requesting reviews from people who do not return reviews in a timely manner or do not provide reasoning for their views, whether harsh or lenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewer policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees may invite a co-reviewer (for example, a junior member of their lab) but should notify the editor of the intention before doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consulting with lab colleagues is acceptable but they should be identified to the editors; consulting outside experts may be acceptable but check with editors first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should respond promptly (normally within two weeks of receiving a manuscript) and inform the editors if they anticipate a longer delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt reviews support rapid editorial decisions; if delays are expected, notify editors so alternatives can be found and authors kept informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and signing reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer identities are not released to authors or other referees, except when referees sign their comments to authors or explicitly agree to release their name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing reports is voluntary; the journal maintains reviewer anonymity by default and will neither confirm nor deny speculation about identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent peer review consent
rubrics_metrics.description: By agreeing to review a manuscript, reviewers give their consent to the potential publication of the reviewer comments made to authors as part of transparent peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can opt out of transparent peer review at completion of peer review before acceptance. Confidential reviewer comments to the editor will not be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing of referees' reports by editors
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of policy, the journal does not suppress referees' reports; any comments intended for the authors are transmitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On rare occasions, editors may edit a report to remove offensive language or comments that reveal confidential information about other matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest disclosure and avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors avoid referees whom the authors have excluded, recent or ongoing collaborators, those who have commented on drafts of the manuscript, direct competitors to publish the same finding, those with a history of dispute with the authors, or those who have a financial or any other interest in the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should draw attention to anything that might affect their review and decline to review if they feel unable to be objective; however, closeness to the field or prior review for another journal does not automatically disqualify someone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to necessary literature
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer does not have access to a published paper necessary for evaluation, the journal will supply the reviewer with a copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send the publication reference to the editor who sent the paper to review; the editor will obtain the paper, paying any necessary fees, and send it to the reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to follow-up reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: When referees agree to review a paper, this is considered a commitment to review subsequent revisions as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will not send resubmitted papers to referees if it seems that the authors have not made a serious attempt to address the referees' criticisms; referees should be willing to provide follow-up advice as requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision context and weighing of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors make decisions based on reviewers' advice but may not follow majority recommendation; they evaluate the strength of arguments and may consider additional information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees are welcome to recommend a course of action but should bear in mind other referees may disagree; set out arguments for and against publication to assist editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback to referees about outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors normally inform referees of decisions and send copies of other referees' reports; referees are normally informed when a paper is accepted despite their negative recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees who are overruled should not assume lack of confidence in their judgment; editors may consult other referees or bring additional reviewers to resolve disputes.
